concept.name: Gamma hedge
concept.definition: An options-hedging technique that neutralizes a position's gamma - the rate at which delta changes per $1 move in the underlying - so that the delta hedge remains effective for larger price moves without constant rebalancing.
concept.intuition: Gamma is how fast your delta hedge goes stale; hedging gamma keeps the hedge from drifting out of alignment every time the underlying moves.
concept.mechanics: Long options (calls or puts) have positive gamma, short options negative gamma, and the underlying itself has zero gamma, so gamma can only be hedged by adding other options: the trader first sets total gamma to zero with a traded option, then restores delta neutrality with the underlying. Gamma is highest for at-the-money options near expiration.
concept.formula: Position gamma = sum over positions of (quantity * multiplier * gamma_i); choose an options position Q such that position gamma + Q * multiplier * gamma_hedge_instrument = 0, then re-neutralize delta.
concept.failure_modes: Gamma hedges are themselves unstable near expiration, when ATM gamma spikes, and require trading additional options with their own costs and vega exposure; a gamma-neutral book still carries higher-order and volatility risk.
concept.misconceptions: You cannot gamma-hedge with the underlying stock - stock positions have no gamma because their delta is fixed at 1 or -1; only options change a position's gamma.
concept.example: A market maker short a 0.50-delta call with gamma 0.06 buys enough of another listed option with gamma 0.03 to bring book gamma to zero, then adjusts shares to restore delta neutrality.

citations.source: The Options Industry Council (OIC), Options Education: Gamma
citations.section: Gamma definition; stock positions have no gamma
